en: The Sūtra of the Five Mothers and Sons, translated by the layman Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi kingdom during the Wu dynasty.
Long ago, there was an arhat who practiced the path in the mountains. There was a small...

At the age of seven, the boy took a great liking to the Way and its teachings; he took leave of his mother to leave the household life and sought ordination as a śrāmaṇera. Following a great śramaṇa in the mountains, he studied the Way, providing for his teacher’s needs, reciting the sūtras, and practicing the Path without ever flagging.
By the age of eight, he attained the eye of wisdom, enabling him to see through to the infinite;
his ears could hear with penetrating clarity, such that all the good and evil deeds performed above and below heaven were heard and known by him;
his body could fly, reaching any destination, where he could divide his single form into many and manifest himself as various beings, accomplishing whatever he wished.
He knows his own past lives and where he has come from; he fully knows all the paths of good and evil traversed by the people and even by the crawling and wriggling creatures.
When he was in a previous life as the mother of five sons, he sat down and laughed to himself.
His teacher asked, "Why do you laugh?"
The śrāmaṇera replied,
"There is nothing to laugh at.
The master said:
"In these mountains there is neither singing nor music; you are merely mocking me.
The śrāmaṇera replied, "I do not dare to mock my teacher; I am merely laughing at myself."

I was the son of five mothers during one lifetime; each mother wept for me day and night, overcome with grief and sorrow that they could not restrain, constantly dwelling on their longing for their child, never once forgetting me.
"I thought only of myself, yet I grieved for the five families [of my kin], and it was for this reason that I laughed; I did not dare to laugh at you, Master.
When I was born as the child of my primary mother, my neighbor likewise gave birth to a son on the very same day as I."
When my mother saw her son coming and going, walking about, she thought with sorrow:
"If my own son were here, he too would be coming and going and walking about like this."
With tears falling like rain from the bitterness of his grief, he spoke these words of sorrow, thinking of his son:
"When I was the son of my second mother, I was short-lived and died prematurely."
When my mother saw others nursing their infants, she thought of me being nursed; overcome with grief, she wept and said, "I am thinking of my son.
When I was the son of my third mother, I died at the age of ten.
As her mother was about to eat, she wept with grief and lamented, saying:
"If my son were here, he too would have eaten with me.
Having abandoned me to die, he leaves me to eat alone."
Choking with sobs, he said, "Think of me!
Furthermore, when I was her son for a fourth time as her mother, my meager lifespan ended first and I died.
When we of our generation took wives, my mother saw them and immediately thought:"
"If my son were still alive, I would have had him take a wife.
He cried out,
"What crime have I committed against Heaven that it should kill my son?"

"Furthermore, when I was the child of my fifth mother, I was seven years old. Having a love for the Way, I took leave of my family, departed from my mother to follow a teacher, entered the mountains to seek the Way, and attained the path of an Arhat."
"My mother weeps every day, saying:

'I bore you as my only son, who followed a teacher to study the Way; yet I know not where you are, nor whether you suffer from hunger or satiety, cold or heat; I know not whether you live or die, for we shall never see one another again.'"
Afflicted with grief and anguish, they thought only of their sons.
These five mothers happened to meet together, and each cried out, "I have lost my son! As they wept against one another, they could not restrain themselves.

"This is my very body and soul, passing through successive births to become children within the wombs of five mothers; this surely confuses people and causes them to weep and go mad with grief. They think only of me as one single person, each wishing to commit suicide."
"This is why I smile.
To give rise to thoughts regarding worldly commoners: they do not know that when one dies, there is a destination where one must be reborn; they all merely speak of 'death.

How could commoners know that after death there is rebirth, that by performing good deeds one naturally receives its blessing, and by committing evil one receives its calamity, such that nothing is lost upon others?"

In this world, they commit all manner of evil deeds without any sense of fear or difficulty; after death, they shall enter the Tai Shan Hell, where the suffering is most extreme, yet then it will be too late for regret to avail them.
I am weary of the world’s toil and suffering; therefore, I have taken leave of my parents to enter the mountains to practice with diligence in pursuit of the Way.
Now, with my own eyes, I behold the animals, hungry ghosts, and those in the hells, and I feel terror on their behalf.
Now, having been graced by the Buddha’s benevolence, I have been able to hear the Dharma of the sutras.

Day and night I feel pity and sorrow for my five mothers, who could not liberate themselves and instead remained anxious; whereas all that I sought and prayed for has now been attained. I contemplate how the people of the world give birth to one another in succession and yet mock one another without ceasing.
The body all returns to the earth, and the soul follows its deeds according to their goodness or evil; none can extricate themselves from this.
Only by severing affection and being able to depart from craving and desire can one attain liberation.

Since I shall no longer encounter birth and death, I regret that this body has been severed; like a person who does not sow seeds, I shall abide in the most blissful path of Nirvana, forever free from toil and suffering.
Having explained this to his teacher, he immediately flew away.
Thus ends the *Buddha-bhāṣita Pañcamātṛputra-sūtra*.
